1:
The three days are counted from the dismissal, not the departure, and the distance is the reason. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) are explicit that it means the third day after David’s dismission by Achish and not after his leaving Ziklag. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) adds the geography: the dismissal can hardly have happened at Shunem, some ninety miles off, so the scene must have fallen somewhere in Philistia after the whole force had gathered. John Gill (reformed) reckons the march home at eighty-eight miles; Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) cites Calmet for more than thirty leagues between Aphek and Ziklag.

Why the raid fell when it did is read providentially and politically. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) finds two corrections in it: the cruelty of Saul’s pity in sparing the Amalekites, since had he destroyed them as he ought these would not have been in being to do the mischief; and a rebuke to David for his forwardness to march with the Philistines, since when we go abroad in the way of our duty we may hope God will keep our families in our absence, but not otherwise.

That the captives were spared at all is the chapter’s first puzzle, and the answers divide. Henry presses it hardest: when David invaded them he put all to the sword, and no reason can be given why they did not retaliate in kind but that God restrained them, who says to the fury of the cruellest men, Hitherto shalt thou come and no further; whether they were kept for triumph, sale or slavery, God designed to use Amalek for the correction and not the destruction of the house of David. Ellicott answers commercially: women and children had a marketable value and were carried off to be sold, probably into Egypt, with which the Amalekites as neighbours had constant dealings. Clarke answers by ignorance — a travelling predatory horde who had plainly not heard what David had done to their tribe, or they would have slain every soul they found.

On the mutiny all six speak, and the causes they assign are cumulative rather than rival. Henry gives two, that the men blamed him for provoking Amalek and leaving Ziklag ungarrisoned, and that they now despaired of the preferment they had promised themselves, hoping ere this to have been all princes and finding themselves all beggars. Keil and Delitzsch say they sought the occasion of the calamity in his connection with Achish, which many of his adherents had very probably disliked. Ellicott sharpens that into the bitter degradation of having marched against their own countrymen under the banner of Gath, so that pent-up fury found its vent. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) lists the counts flatly: coming to Ziklag at first, provoking the Amalekites, marching away with Achish, and leaving the families unguarded. Clarke reads their temper instead: David had done much to civilise these men, yet here is the unruly and ferocious spirit of them, and yet they strongly felt the ties of natural affection and grieved every man for his sons and daughters.

The closing clause draws out what each takes encouragement to mean. Henry sets it against the men’s fretting: the soul of the people was bitter, and their impatience added wormwood to the affliction, but while they gave liberty to their passions he set his graces on work, considering God’s providence and the particular promises made to him, so that when he was at his wits’ end he was not at his faith’s end. Clarke grounds it in a clear conscience, this evil having come through neither his neglect nor his folly. Ellicott makes it prayer and reaches for a contrast: David threw himself on the mercy of the God who had chosen him, while at about this same hour Saul, alone and distrustful, fought and fell on the bloody day of Gilboa.
7:
Three voices read the call for the ephod as the repair of an omission. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) holds that if David had priest and ephod with him in the Philistine camp it was a great neglect not to have enquired about his engagement to Achish, perhaps being ashamed to own his religion so far among the uncircumcised; he now apprehends the trouble was brought to correct that oversight, so the first thing he does is call for the ephod. It is well if we get this good by our afflictions, to be reminded of neglected duties. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) has him sensible of his former error, necessity bringing him to his duty and his duty meeting with success. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) presses furthest: through all the wanderings we hear nothing of prayer or of consulting the Urim, and David seems to have determined the Philistine sojourn entirely of himself, one unbroken series of sin and calamity being the result.

Ellicott alone defends the Urim as the actual medium of the answer. Modern commentators, he says, prefer to disbelieve in any response through it, passing the transaction over or assuming some inspiration came to the high priest when vested; but the plain sense of the frequent references is that the divine will was made known through it, and the case of Saul distinguishes being answered by Urim from a dream, a vision or a prophet. He grants the Talmudic traditions are in places fanciful, yet calls it arbitrary to reject the ancient belief of the Hebrew race about the gems for a reading that fits the text lamely. Wesley attends to the manner rather than the medium: formerly God answered slowly and gradually, but now speedily and at once because the business required haste — so gracious is he that he considers even the degree of our necessities.

The two hundred left at the brook are read as a trial and as a kindness. Henry makes it both: a trial of David’s faith, whether he could go on depending on the word of God when a third of his men failed him, and an instance of his tenderness, that he would by no means urge them beyond their strength — the Son of David likewise considering the frame of followers who are not all alike vigorous, for where we are weak there he is kind. John Gill (reformed) and Wesley both make the pursuit itself the act of faith, four hundred being a small number against an enemy whose strength he did not know; Gill notes that as many afterwards escaped on camels as David had men with him. Ellicott takes the six hundred for the veteran band whose speed and endurance he could depend on. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) adds that they were appointed to guard the baggage.

On the abandoned slave the comment converges on providence and the master’s cruelty. Henry is sharpest: that master has the spirit of an Amalekite and not of an Israelite who can use a servant worse than a beast, and the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel; justly did Providence make this abused servant the instrument of a whole army’s destruction, for God hears the cry of oppressed servants. Clarke calls the desertion inhuman when they had asses enough, and says God visited it upon them. Wesley finds the providence further back, that the lad was not of the cursed race appointed to destruction but an Egyptian who might be spared: there is no fighting against God, who can make the smallest accidents serviceable to the greatest effects. Ellicott calls the abandonment a needless barbarity, given the camels in their train. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) keep to the relief itself, the slice of fig-cake and the raisin-cakes, after which his spirit of life returned to him.
16:
Which twilight is meant divides all four who touch it, and each gives a reason. John Gill (reformed) lays out the options: some take the morning, so that David came by night, let them alone till they were drunk and asleep, and fell on them early, as Josephus relates it; others the evening, with the Targum; and some read the morrow as following two evenings, carrying the slaughter into a third day. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) settle it lexically for the evening, holding that the word means the evening twilight here and not the dawn, a sense not even sustained by the one passage urged for it. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reports their view but prefers Bishop Hervey’s, that the contrast drawn between twilight and evening rather suggests the morning: David arrived at night, deferred the attack till dawn when they would still be sleeping off the debauch, and was then held all day by their numbers. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) argues for the evening on two grounds: feasting and dancing are evening work, and darkness kept the fewness of his force from being seen.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) twice declines to let the slaughter be justified too easily, and is alone in doing so. That these Amalekites were enemies of the Philistines is evident, he grants, but it does not follow that the people David destroyed were enemies too — too hastily assumed, he says, by Dr Chandler and others, the better to vindicate David’s character. And though Amalek was a proscribed nation, so that David has been supposed in extirpating them to fulfil the express will of God, that depends on whether he had an express commission from God himself, as Saul had.

The carelessness of the camp is read as the cause of its ruin. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the moral twice over: sinners are nearest to ruin when they cry peace and safety and put the evil day far from them, and nothing gives our spiritual enemies more advantage than sensuality, eating and drinking and dancing having been the soft and pleasant way in which many have gone down to the congregation of the dead; so the triumphing of the wicked is short, and wrath comes on them, as on Belshazzar, in the midst of their jollity. He supposes the revelry was held in honour of their idol-gods, to whom they gave the praise of their success, and reads the whole recovery as a resemblance to the Son of David, who took the prey from the mighty and led captivity captive. Wesley accounts for the security circumstantially: they were almost home, both armies were engaged elsewhere, and David they believed was with them, so they had no visible cause of danger and were then nearest destruction. Ellicott imagines it from the other side, the veterans looking on the revel and remembering whose homes had been laid waste to furnish the spoil Amalek was rejoicing over, then falling on the robbers with a fury that carried them against far greater numbers.

The drovers’ cry is both a textual crux and a reversal. Keil and Delitzsch call the verse obscure and resolve it by distinguishing the herds: the Amalekites’ own sheep and oxen were driven in front of the cattle recovered from them, and the drovers called the foremost David’s booty. Ellicott reaches the same reading, blames the italicised word in the English for obscuring it, and finds David’s motive in choosing flocks and herds — for warriors the least desirable share — plain from what he does with them next. Wesley and Henry both mark the turn in the men: those who lately spoke of stoning him now magnify him and celebrate his praise, Henry adding that they got by him more than they had lost, so that the world and its sentiments are governed by interest.
21:
The greeting is read as deliberate kindness. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) notes that the two hundred came out to congratulate a success they could not contribute to, since we should rejoice in a good work done though Providence has laid us aside; and that David, far from upbraiding their weakness, asked them of peace, having left them faint and unwell, or bade them be of good cheer and lose nothing by staying behind — which is what they seemed afraid of. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) has him salute them with all kindly courtesy, and the camp’s harmony broken immediately after.

What broke it is named sharply. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) glosses the phrase for men of Belial as the common expression for the sour, the rugged, the severe, the idle and the profane. John Gill (reformed) calls them ill-natured and covetous, and reads their answer as implying that the two hundred had asked for a share. Henry is harshest: probably the same men who had spoken of stoning David now spoke of defrauding their brethren, and a while ago they would gladly have given half their own to recover the other half, yet having all their own they are not content without their brethren’s too — so soon do men forget their low estate. To return the wives and children without the goods was to give them the mouths without the meat; those are men of Belial indeed who delight in putting hardships on their brethren and care not who is starved so they may be fed to the full.

David’s grounds are gratitude and justice. Henry supplies both: the spoil is what God has given, to be used under his direction, and God’s mercy to us should make us merciful to one another; while in justice the two hundred stayed behind for want of strength and not of good-will, which was their misfortune and not their fault, they had done their part in former actions, and even now did good service guarding what somebody had to guard — for every post of service is not alike a post of honour, yet those serviceable in a meaner station ought to share, as every member of the body has its use and so its share of the nourishment. Henry, John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) and Gill all three remark on the address: he overruled them, but calling them brethren and owning them as fellow-soldiers, managing his authority with sweetness while keeping his dignity as general — superiors, Henry adds, often lose their authority by haughtiness but seldom by courtesy. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) keep to the grammar, taking the particle for the accusative sign and not the preposition, and one written form for a copyist’s error.

Whether the rule begins here is genuinely disputed. Gill reports that the Hebrew reads upwards, of old, so that Jarchi makes it a statute already of Abraham’s day from which David learnt it, though Josephus is express that the law obtained from David’s own time. Clarke and Henry both point to earlier precedent — the division of the spoil of Midian, and Abraham quitting his title to the spoils of Sodom by the law of war — though Henry still calls it a statute of distributions of the first year of David’s reign. Clarke takes the words unto this day for another indication that the book was composed long after the events. Ellicott traces it forward: the decision remained in force until the Maccabees, and he sets beside it the scene in Polybius where Scipio, after taking Nova Carthago, divided the spoil equally among the troops engaged, the reserves, the sick, and those detached on special service. Wesley cites the same Roman practice, and gives the reason: the reserve shares the hazard, stands ready for a retreat, and is in actual service where its general placed it.
26:
Why the presents went out is answered the same way by all: gratitude and policy. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) puts it most briefly, partly in gratitude for former favours and partly in policy, to engage their affections. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) has these for the people among whom he sojourned in exile, who had given him shelter and protection, so that gratitude required it. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) press the policy: the gifts could not fail to make these elders well disposed, and so to ease his recognition as king after Saul’s death, which followed immediately; some of the places, they add, may themselves have been plundered, Amalek having invaded the Negeb of Judah. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) agrees these must be the towns where he and his followers had been kindly received in the long wanderings.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) divides the act three ways. There is generosity, since he aimed not to enrich himself but to serve his country, and God afterwards enriched him and set him to rule the country he had served. There is piety, for he calls the gift a blessing — no present being a comfort to our friends but as God’s blessing makes it so, which intimates that his prayers went with it — and he sends it from the spoil of the enemies of the Lord, so calling them rather than his own enemies, that the receivers might rejoice in the victory for the Lord’s sake. And there is policy, to engage his countrymen to appear for him at an accession he now saw at hand, since a man’s gift makes room for him, munificence recommending a man more than magnificence. Henry notices too who got nothing: the Ziphites had none of these presents, nor the men of Keilah, which shows that though he was such a saint as not to revenge affronts he was not such a fool as not to take notice of them.

Which Bethel is meant divides them four ways. John Gill (reformed) rejects the Bethel of Benjamin for Kirjathjearim, called Bethel because the ark was there. Clarke places it in Ephraim. Ellicott takes it for Bethuel or Bethul in Simeon, noting that the Greek reads another name altogether. Keil and Delitzsch only rule out the famous Bethel. Henry makes the name the point rather than the site: Bethel signifies the house of God, and that place is served first for its name’s sake, or else what is meant is not the city but wherever the ark then was, and thither David sent the first and best, for the sake of him who is first and best. On Aroer the two contradict each other outright, Clarke putting it beyond Jordan on the Arnon in the tribe of Gad, and Gill refusing that identification because David is never said to have been there, so that some city of the name in Judah must be meant; Ellicott, without arguing it, describes colossal ruins south of Hebron.

Ellicott closes with an observation he credits to Bishop Hervey, and it is the most telling thing said about the list: it is a remarkable proof of David’s grateful nature and his fidelity to early friendships that among the men he employed in offices of trust at the height of his power we find so many inhabitants of these obscure places — Ezri the son of Shemei the Ramathite, Zabdi the Shiphmite, and many besides, the friends of his youth. Ellicott traces two himself, taking the officer over the vineyards for a native of Ramah of the South and the keeper of the cellars for a man of Siphmoth. Henry makes a quieter point of the order, that Hebron comes last because thither he sent the residuum, which was the largest share, having an eye already on the place as fittest for his head-quarters.
